name: Electric Power Research Institute, Inc.
headquarters: 3420 Hillview Avenue, Palo Alto, California 94304 (Form 990 principal office); principal offices and laboratories also in Charlotte, North Carolina; Knoxville, Tennessee; and Lenox, Massachusetts (Schedule O), with offices in Dallas and Washington, D.C., and EPRI Europe DAC in Dublin
employees: 1,475 (Form 990 FY2024, Part I line 5); 1,455 (FY2023); 1,373 (FY2022); the About page says 'more than 1,300 employees'

ownership.notes: A non-stock, non-profit corporation with no owners. Legal domicile: the Form 990 header gives 'State of legal domicile: DC' through the FY2024 return (filed 2025-11-14) and Schedule O cites 'the Nonprofit Corporation Code of the District of Columbia'; the certificate of incorporation and bylaws EPRI now posts describe 'a Non-Stock, Nonprofit Delaware Corporation' with its registered office at 1209 Orange Street, Wilmington, and California registered a new foreign-corporation branch of a Delaware EPRI in 2026 — a redomestication whose date neither document states. California is only the principal-office state (Wikipedia's 'California' incorporation is wrong). EIN 23-7175375; IRS ruling September 1972; governed by a 37-member board elected by five membership classes, with permanent seats for the Tennessee Valley Authority and the Bonneville Power Administration

summary: BOTTOM LINE UP FRONT: EPRI is the utility industry's own USD 500-million-a-year research cooperative — a 501(c)(3) funded about half by fixed annual membership dues from utilities that 'represent 90% of the electricity generated and delivered in the United States' and half by supplemental projects those members and others buy into — and since October 2024 it has run DCFlex, the one forum where the hyperscalers (Google, Meta, Microsoft, Oracle, NVIDIA), the data-centre landlords (Compass, QTS) and the utilities and grid operators (Duke, Constellation, Southern, Dominion, PG&E, ERCOT, PJM) test together whether an AI campus can be a flexible load; its BESS Failure Incident Database is the statistic every battery-safety conversation in this corpus quotes. BACKGROUND. Founded 1972 by Chauncey Starr after the 1965 Northeast blackout; a District of Columbia non-profit corporation through its FY2024 Form 990, now presenting Delaware governing documents; principal office Palo Alto with laboratories in Charlotte, Knoxville and Lenox. Finances (audited, Deloitte): total revenues USD 509.6 million in 2025 (491.7 million in 2024; 466.6 million in 2023), of which membership USD 244.4 million and supplemental USD 261.8 million; a USD 6.7 million surplus in 2025 after deficits of 10.6 million (2024) and 14.0 million (2023); net assets USD 153.6 million. Form 990 FY2024: total revenue USD 503,197,591, expenses 516,331,444, 1,475 employees, CEO Arshad Mansoor paid USD 2,132,369 plus 737,890 other. Members: 'more than 450 companies in 45 countries'; research organised in four sectors (Nuclear — about USD 184 million of 2025 expense — Generation, Energy Delivery & Customer Solutions, Technology Innovation) across 99 programmes in the 2026 portfolio, including Program 94 Energy Storage and Distributed Generation (USD 5.5 million, 2026). Data-centre work runs through the DCFlex supplemental project (launched 29 October 2024 with 15 founding members; 'more than 60 companies' by February 2026; nine demonstration sites; a published price list from USD 50,000 to USD 325,000 a year by funder type), the Open Power AI Consortium (20 March 2025, with NVIDIA), Flex MOSAIC (March 2026) and the Powering Intelligence load forecasts (9–17 percent of US electricity by 2030, February 2026). Collection gaps: the Delaware redomestication date, the DCFlex membership roster in full, per-programme revenue, and whether DCFlex's 'public' deliverables are readable without an EPRI.com account (four were not).
ecosystemRole: The corpus's eleventh `advisor` and the only non-profit among them: where DNV, UL Solutions and Intertek sell certificates and independent-engineer reports to one client at a time, EPRI sells collaborative research to the utilities that buy from and interconnect everyone else in this corpus — the gatekeepers — and publishes the parts of it that set the industry's shared facts: the failure-rate statistics behind every BESS safety argument ('9.2 incidents per gigawatt in 2018 to 0.2 per gigawatt in 2023'; '72% of failures … within two years'), the data-centre load forecast regulators and DOE cite, the Flex MOSAIC flexibility classes, the ESIC commissioning guides and the DER-VET storage valuation tool. Its seat in the AI-power chain is DCFlex: EPRI 'oversees' the demonstrations in which Emerald AI, Oracle, NVIDIA and Salt River Project cut a GPU cluster's draw 25 percent for three hours, Google and Duke choreograph workloads in Lenoir, and National Grid and Nebius curtail an AI cluster in London — the evidence on which 'flexible large load' tariffs and interconnection rules are being written. Independence: EPRI 'do[es] not advocate for any specific company, sector, or technology', but its funding is the utilities' and 'the vast majority of its board members are utility executives' (Energy & Policy Institute), with an NVIDIA executive seated as an external director since 2025. Assurance seat decision: EPRI tests (battery burn tests, the HVO backup-generator field test, the DER interoperability lab), writes guidelines and runs ESIC, but it issues no certificate, listing or lender's report — the `assurance` adjacent seat is granted on the testing-and-guidelines line and the basis says so.

productsAndServices.name: Research programmes — the membership product (99 programmes, four sectors)
productsAndServices.description: A fixed-price annual membership that buys a seat on programme committees ('Each member company that invests in a research program is entitled to appoint committee members to represent it'), the programme's deliverables (reports, software, databases, training), and 'the support of EPRI researchers and technical advisors'. The 2026 portfolio lists 99 programmes across Nuclear, Generation, Energy Delivery & Customer Solutions and Technology Innovation, plus the Low-Carbon Resources Initiative and Climate READi workstreams. Membership revenue: USD 244.4 million (2025), 238.5 million (2024), 237.1 million (2023) — about 48 percent of revenue; 'Existing Product Credits' accrue only to multi-year members.
highlights: Governance of the product (EPRI's words): 'Program Committees — Work with us within each research program to define scope, assess priorities, and determine the best mechanisms to deliver the results of our work'; 'More than 1,400 leaders and technical experts from the electricity sector, academia and government help EPRI develop and conduct its research'.

Program 94 Energy Storage and Distributed Generation (ED&CS; 2026 budget '$5.5M'): 'advance the integration and use of safe, reliable, affordable, environmentally responsible energy storage, distributed generation, and microgrids'; members gain 'technology evaluation, economic and technical modeling, testing and field demonstration, safety practices … community engagement'; deliverables named — the Energy Storage Roadmap, ESIC ('eighteen published guidelines, tools, and templates'), DER-VET®, the Energy Storage Technology Database (with P221 Bulk Energy Storage), lithium-ion combustion-product burn tests, First Responder Engagement Guidance, the Utility Battery Energy Storage Handbook, StorageWiki with the failure-incident database.

Nuclear is the largest sector by expense (USD 184.4 million of 513.5 million in 2025): '~$200 million USD in annual funding to support the industry through nuclear R&D'; '150+ Nuclear Deliverables … issued annually'; '$89 – the additional leverage that an average full nuclear member gets for every $1 of funding towards base projects' (Nuclear Sector Value Briefing, August 2025).

Membership classes (Schedule O): Class I US federal, cooperative, public-power and RTO members (elect eight directors; TVA and BPA each appoint one), Class II regulated domestic utilities (seventeen), Class III non-US utilities and ISOs (six), Class IV non-voting unregulated generators, Class V non-voting others 'supporting a domestic or international program for electric sector research'; the Governance and Nominating Committee appoints seven.

Reach, as stated: 'EPRI's trusted experts collaborate with more than 450 companies in 45 countries'; members 'represent 90% of the electricity generated and delivered in the United States' (2020 boilerplate; relayed since as EPRI's self-description); 'With more than 1,300 employees' (About) against 1,475 on the FY2024 Form 990.
productsAndServices.positioning: The only industry-wide cooperative of its kind in US electricity; 'Rigorously objective in our role and our research, we do not advocate for any specific company, sector, or technology.' The Energy & Policy Institute's critique (August 2025) is the counter-position: about half the funding is utility dues and 'the vast majority of its board members are utility executives'.
productsAndServices.soldThrough: Direct annual membership agreements with utilities and other eligible organisations, priced on member size (T&D throughput bands appear in the DCFlex price list); multi-year contracts earn Existing Product Credits.
targetSegments: Public power, cooperatives and federal utilities
productsAndServices.roadmap: The 2026 portfolio is live; a VP for 'AI Power and Data Center Innovation' now sits on the leadership page, signalling a standalone data-centre line beyond the DCFlex supplemental.

productsAndServices.name: Supplemental projects and the DCFlex Data Center Flexible Load Initiative
productsAndServices.description: Supplemental projects are the second revenue line, larger than membership since 2024 (USD 261.8 million in 2025; 250.2 million in 2024; 228.0 million in 2023): opt-in, separately funded projects 'offered twice yearly', with 25 percent of a member's annual research funding allocated to self-directed or tailored-collaboration accounts that can be spent on them; non-members may fund them. DCFlex (Project 01-119727) is the flagship: launched 29 October 2024 'to explore how data centers can support the electric grid, enable better asset utilization, improve interconnection, and support the clean energy transition', planned as 'a 3-year initiative … completed by the end of 2027', with five workstreams and nine demonstration sites by February 2026.
highlights: Price list (DCFlex Supplemental Project Notice, September 2025, verbatim): 'Utilities *Large $250K; *Medium $175K; *Small $75K; Generation only $200K; Data Center Developers/Operators $325K; Technology Providers $250K; ISOs, RTOs, and Others $50K; Mgmt Consultant $200k' per year, with utility size set by 'Transmission and Distribution Throughput Basis: Large - T>10,000 or D>44,000; Medium - 10,000>T>5,000 or 44,000>D>15,000; Small - T<5,000 or D<15,000'.

Founding members (29 October 2024): 'Compass Datacenters, Constellation Energy, Duke Energy, the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT), Google, Meta, New York Power Authority, NRG Energy, NVIDIA, Pacific Gas and Electric Company (PG&E), PJM Interconnection, Portland General Electric, QTS Data Centers, Southern Company, and Vistra Corp.' Growth: 'nearly 40 participants, including Dominion Energy, ERCOT, PJM, Google, Microsoft, and Nvidia' (Latitude Media, March 2025, with RTE, ING and PPC joining); 'more than 40 members' (EPRI testimony, June 2025); 'over 45 companies' (August 2025); 'more than 60 companies' (February 2026); Flex MOSAIC 'developed … in collaboration with more than 65' organisations (March 2026); '70+' member logos on dcflex.epri.com.

Demonstrations: Lenoir, North Carolina (Google and Duke Energy — workload choreography); Phoenix, Arizona (Emerald AI with Oracle, NVIDIA, Databricks, Salt River Project — 'a 25% reduction in cluster power usage for three hours during peak grid events while maintaining AI quality of service', arXiv 2507.00909, 1 July 2025; 256 GPUs); Paris (Data4 with Schneider Electric and RTE — UPS grid support); and, announced 2 February 2026: Chicago (Google and NVIDIA — AI compute flexibility 'in a simulated production environment'), Dallas (HVO renewable diesel in Compass backup generators — public report 29 July 2026), Ashburn–Chicago (geospatial load shifting), Manassas (Compass; 'flexibility by design at commercial scale' — the 96 MW Aurora AI Factory with NVIDIA and Emerald AI, 'late 2026'), London (National Grid, Emerald AI, Nebius, NVIDIA — 'cutting load by up to 30–40% within seconds'), Texas (PADO AI compute-and-HVAC control). A December 2025 GPU-cluster demonstration 'achieved 100% compliance with 200+ power targets, delivering 40% load reductions in under one minute' (EPRI Journal).

Flex MOSAIC (23 March 2026, CERAWeek): 'a uniform flexibility classification framework for large electric loads' — 'a small set of uniform flexibility classes' (five) — with NERC's Jim Robb and NARUC's Ann Rendahl endorsing; Mansoor: flexibility 'is becoming the third leg of the speed-to-power stool, alongside generation and transmission'; final version planned 'by October 2026'.

Deliverables (40-plus on dcflex.epri.com, all labelled public): the Reliability Guideline for Emerging Large Loads (December 2025), the Data Center Load Shape Library and web tool, the Retail Flexible Load Tariff dataset ('159 flexible load tariffs from 71 U.S. utilities'), 'Texas SB6 Explained', the Global Survey of Data Center Owners & Operators ('1,126 data center professionals across twelve countries', August 2026), the PJM capacity-crunch Quick Insight. Access caveat: four 'public' PDFs returned 'your company has not purchased the rights to view this item' to an anonymous download — public here means free to registered EPRI.com accounts.
productsAndServices.positioning: The only multi-party test bed for data-centre flexibility with hyperscalers, landlords, utilities and grid operators in one project; the Duke Nicholas Institute's 'Rethinking Load Growth' (76–126 GW of headroom at 0.25–1% curtailment) is the academic companion, not an EPRI product. Sceptics on the record: AES's Kleber Costa ('Data center operators do not like to be flexible'), Schneider's Steven Carlini ('it's questionable whether they want to do it'); EPRI's own Anuja Ratnayake: 'If it is banking services or credit card services, there is very little flexibility.'
productsAndServices.soldThrough: Supplemental project funding agreements by funder type (price list above); members may apply self-directed or tailored-collaboration funds; demonstrations hosted by participating companies at their own sites.
productsAndServices.roadmap: Testing 'could run through 2027'; the Manassas 96 MW Aurora site online 'late 2026'; Flex MOSAIC final framework by October 2026; ride-through testing and certification methodologies under development (EPRI Journal, August 2026).

productsAndServices.name: Open Power AI Consortium, SAFERai.power and the AI initiatives
productsAndServices.category: Consortia — AI for the power sector
productsAndServices.description: The Open Power AI Consortium (launched 20 March 2025 at NVIDIA GTC) 'to drive the development and deployment of an open AI model tailored for the power sector' — domain-specific models built with Articul8 and NVIDIA and served as an NVIDIA NIM microservice in early access, a sandbox, '130+ free to use datasets', the WattWorks benchmarking hub — with membership 'of EPRI member and non-member utilities, academia, research organizations and national labs, technology companies, hyperscalers and AI infrastructure service providers' contributing 'active participation … sharing data and insights, providing financial and in-kind contributions'; no fee schedule published. SAFERai.power (August 2026) adds an AI risk framework with 'more than two dozen founding' members.
highlights: Launch roster (EPRI release): energy executives from 'ACWA (NOMAC), Alliant Energy, Ameren, Constellation, Con Edison, CPS Energy, Dairyland Power Cooperative, Duke Energy, ENOWA … Exelon, GCC Interconnection Authority, Georgia Transmission Corporation, KEPCO, KHNP, Khalifa University, MISO, North Carolina's Electric Cooperatives, New York Power Authority (NYPA), Pacific Gas and Electric Company (PG&E), Portland General Electric, PPL Corporation, RTE, Santee Cooper, Saudi Electricity Company, Southern Company, Southern California Edison, Tennessee Valley Authority, WEC Energy Group, and Westinghouse Electric Company' with 'key technology companies Articul8, AWS, Linux Foundation Energy, Microsoft, NVIDIA, Oracle, Rolls-Royce SMR Limited, SHI and WWT'.

Scale as EPRI states it: '300+ Organizations Engaged', '150+ Technology Providers', '120+ Utilities/Energy Companies', '30+ AI Models' (openpowerai.org); '250+' use cases compiled (POWER, August 2025); later joiners Avangrid, Cisco, GE Vernova, Google, Burns & McDonnell, KYRO AI, Landis+Gyr. Check: no open-weights release exists on Hugging Face or GitHub as of 4 October 2026 — the models remain NIM early access.

First output: 'EPRI Publishes First Electric Sector Benchmarking Results of Public LLMs' (9 December 2025) — '2,100+ questions and answers generated by 94 power sector experts across 35 topics'; GPT-5, Grok 4 and Gemini 2.5 Pro scored 83–86 percent on multiple choice with a '27-percentage-point average accuracy drop' on open-ended questions.

SAFERai.power (6 August 2026): founders include 'Alliant, Ameren, ATC, Arizona Public Service, Centerpoint Energy, Con Edison, Constellation, Cooperative Energy, CPS Energy, Duke Energy, Exelon, HData, Microsoft, MISO, NERC, Nebraska Public Power District, NYPA, NVIDIA, Omaha Public Power District, Pacific Gas & Electric, PJM Interconnection, Salt River Project, SHI International, Southern California Edison, Southern Company, TVA, WEC Energy Group, World Wide Technology'; deliverables a risk framework, evidence packages and an open-source assessment tool.

Adjacent: the micro-data-centre collaboration with NVIDIA, Prologis and InfraPartners (3 February 2026) — '5 to 20 megawatts … at or near utility substations', 'at least five pilot sites in development across the U.S. by the end of 2026'.
productsAndServices.positioning: The utility industry's collective answer to vendor-led AI; NVIDIA is co-developer, consortium member, DCFlex founder and board member (Marc Spieler, external director since April 2025) — the one technology company present at every layer.
productsAndServices.soldThrough: Consortium membership (in-kind, data and financial contributions; EPRI members and non-members); outputs via NVIDIA NIM early access, the WattWorks hub and openpowerai.org.
targetSegments: AI vendors to the power sector
productsAndServices.roadmap: AI for Power Challenge (May 2026); model release beyond NIM early access unannounced; SAFERai.power risk framework and assessment tool in development.

productsAndServices.name: Energy storage safety research — BESS Failure Incident Database, ESIC, StorageWiki, DER-VET and StorageVET
productsAndServices.category: Collaborative research and public tools — energy storage
productsAndServices.description: The storage line sits in Program 94 Energy Storage and Distributed Generation (2026 budget USD 5.5m) and Program 221 Bulk Energy Storage, and most of its output is free to the public: the BESS Failure Incident Database ('initiated in 2021 following the series of lithium ion BESS fires in South Korea and the Surprise, AZ, incident'; events back to 2011), the Energy Storage Integration Council (ESIC, formed 2013, 'eighteen published guidelines, tools, and templates'), StorageWiki, the Battery Storage Fire Safety Roadmap, the open-source DER-VET optimisation tool (an extension of the 2016 StorageVET) and the Energy Storage Test Manual and data-submission guidelines. Funders get project access by login; 'many outputs are publicly released'.
highlights: The failure-rate statistics every BESS safety argument in this corpus leans on: 'Between 2018 and 2023, the global grid-scale BESS failure rate has dropped 97%' (2024 White Paper, free PDF); 9.2 incidents per gigawatt in 2018 to 0.2 in 2023, eight incidents worldwide in 2024 against a 53 percent rise in deployment (as cited in the California Energy Commission docket 25-OPT-02, February 2026); 'dropping 98% from 2018 to 2024' (EPRI-authored chapter in kWh Analytics' Solar Risk Assessment 2025); the live database page now says 99 percent 2018–2025.

Root cause: the TWAICE/EPRI/PNNL study (15 May 2024) analysed 81 incidents, 26 with enough information to assign a cause; '72% of failures in systems whose age is known occurred during construction, the commissioning process or within two years of becoming operational' — 'integration, assembly and construction' led the assigned causes, not cells.

Government reliance: DOE's Energy Storage Safety Strategic Plan (April 2024) cites the ESIC Energy Storage Commissioning Guide and seated EPRI alongside UL Solutions, CSA Group and DNV on its advisory board; the California Energy Commission's final report CEC-500-2024-010 (February 2024) validated DER-VET ('downloaded by over 200 unique users') and recorded 'over 60 monthly task force meetings' run through ESIC.

Burn testing: 'Performed battery module burn testing to identify and quantify emitted gases and particulate matter' (P94); Lithium Ion Combustion Product Characterization; First Responder Engagement Guidance; Utility Battery Energy Storage Handbook; Decommissioning and Recycling Assessment (Cedartown case study).

Partnerships: MOU with Energy Storage Canada (29 September 2025); the CMBlu organic-flow pilot at WEC Energy's Valley plant (2023) 'in collaboration with' EPRI; Energy Dome feasibility studies listed under Bulk Energy Storage.
productsAndServices.positioning: The reference dataset, not a certificate: EPRI records and analyses incidents and writes guidelines, while UL 9540A tests are run by UL Solutions, TÜV and others and listings are issued by certification bodies — EPRI issues none. Its StorageWiki entry on Moss Landing ('300 MW / 1,200 MWh … LG Energy Solution … 4.1 years old') is the neutral record the trade press cites.
productsAndServices.soldThrough: Programme membership (P94, P221) and supplemental funding; ESIC 'Membership is open'; the database, white papers, roadmap and DER-VET are free downloads; non-members can buy reports ('SALE OF R&D REPORTS 752,871', FY2024 Form 990).
targetSegments: Fire marshals, first responders and permitting authorities
Insurers and independent engineers who cite the database
productsAndServices.roadmap: 2026 P94 objectives: 'Safety hazard investigation', 'Performance and reliability assessment — Develop databases', end-of-life and second-use research, critical-materials supply chain.

productsAndServices.name: Powering Intelligence — data-centre load forecasts and the large-load research corpus
productsAndServices.category: Public research — load forecasting and grid integration
productsAndServices.description: The forecast the US power system argues over: Powering Intelligence (May 2024) put data centres at 4.6–9.1 percent of US generation by 2030; the 2026 update (26 February 2026, report 3002034696) raised it to 9–17 percent (380–790 TWh) from a 4–5 percent 2024 base, 'about 60% higher than EPRI projected in 2024', with Virginia at 41–59 percent of state load and AI at 15–25 percent of data-centre electricity. Around it sit the joint report with Epoch AI (11 August 2025: 'training a leading model could require more than 4 gigawatts (GW) of power by 2030'), the state-level projections PNNL republished as the 'IM3 + EPRI Data Center Load Projections' dataset (December 2025), Texas SB6 Explained, the Reliability Guideline for Emerging Large Loads (December 2025) and the FERC co-location technical-conference summary.
highlights: How government cites it: DOE's Office of Electricity web page — 'EPRI estimates that data centers could grow to consume up to 9% of U.S. electricity generation annually by 2030'; LBNL's Large Load Literature Review (November 2025) catalogues six EPRI items and an EPRI utility survey finding 'almost half of the utilities have data center interconnection requests that exceed 50% of their present system peak demand'.

Position on the pipeline: 'announced nominal capacity for data center projects should be treated as a pipeline indicator rather than a near-term peak forecast'; on supply: 'Under current state and federal policies, natural gas dominates near-term incremental supply… if data centers adopt and achieve 24/7 carbon-free energy targets, renewable and battery additions dominate'.

Gas-turbine lead times, as EPRI's Bobby Noble states them: 'orders having a lead time as long as seven years, but most of them are in that five-year period' (August 2025); large turbines 'more than five years', small '18 to 36 months', prices 'from roughly $2,000/kW to $3,000/kW' in six months (March 2026). No EPRI statement on transformer lead times was found.

Reliability work: ride-through curves published or proposed by 'ERCOT, SPP, AESO, RTE, Fingrid, EirGrid, and Energinet' catalogued (EPRI Journal, August 2026); 'Managing Oscillating Load Impacts from Data Centers on Synchronous Machines'; 'Assessing Subsynchronous Torsional Interactions with Respect to AI Training Loads'; 'state regulators approved 29 large-load tariffs in 2025' and a dataset of '159 flexible load tariffs from 71 U.S. utilities'.

Nuclear-and-data-centre line: 'Advanced Nuclear Technology: A Guide for Co-locating Data Centers with Nuclear Plants' (April 2025); Jeremy Renshaw's House Science testimony (12 June 2025); a Nuclear and Data Center Integration Workshop (July 2025).
productsAndServices.positioning: The industry's own forecast rather than a consultancy's — cited by DOE, LBNL, PNNL and the CEC because its authors are the utilities' research arm; its ranges are wide by design and the 2026 revision moved the whole band up.
productsAndServices.soldThrough: Public reports and briefs (free PDFs via restservice.epri.com; some 'public' DCFlex items require epri.com registration); underlying programme work funded by members.
productsAndServices.roadmap: Powering Intelligence refreshes roughly every two years; Flex MOSAIC final framework by October 2026; a VP for AI Power and Data Center Innovation now owns the line.

productsAndServices.name: Laboratories, testing, training and technical services
productsAndServices.description: Laboratories in Charlotte (North Carolina), Knoxville (Tennessee) and Lenox (Massachusetts) do the physical work behind the research: battery-module burn tests, the Nondestructive Evaluation Performance Demonstration Lab ('approximately $20M in samples for the industry' used to qualify inspectors under 10 CFR 50.55a Appendix VIII), the DER Interoperability Lab at Knoxville (August 2026), the DCFlex Dallas field test of renewable diesel (HVO) in a Compass backup generator (public report, 29 July 2026). 'BILLABLE SERVICES' were USD 18,198,066 on the FY2024 Form 990. Training: 'Hundreds of on-demand technical training modules'; 'More than 40,000 professional development hours (PDH) earned by Members through training interactions over the last two years' (nuclear).
highlights: Software suites delivered as member benefits: StorageVET and DER-VET (storage), DCFlex Load Shape Library web tool (July 2026), WattWorks AI benchmarking hub, Tech Radar and Tech Portal (Technology Innovation), and for nuclear the Phoenix Architect suite, Radwaste Hub and the IDKVP digital twin.

Federal cost-reimbursable work is a growing line: 'cost-reimbursable federal and state contracts and grants' revenue USD 67.3m (2025), 34.4m (2024), 27.5m (2023) per the audited statements; USAspending shows DOE obligations of USD 181.3m from October 2019 to September 2026, with a USD 75.1m spike in FY2024; USD 428,000 of FY2025 federal expenditure is excluded pending 'termination appeals with the U.S. Department of Energy' on five awards.

Events: EPRI Summer Seminar, European Workshop Week, Technology Transfer Awards, Incubatenergy Labs Challenge; EPRI Europe DAC (Dublin) runs FLEXIT and DCFlex in Europe; EPRI Gulf serves the GCC members.
productsAndServices.positioning: Member-funded capability rather than a competitive testing business — EPRI does not seek accreditation as a certification body and its laboratories qualify people and characterise hazards rather than list products.
productsAndServices.soldThrough: Programme membership, supplemental funding, cost-reimbursable federal and state contracts, and billable services to members.
productsAndServices.roadmap: DER Interoperability Lab and working group (Knoxville, 2026); ride-through 'testing and certification methodologies' under development in DCFlex — the one place EPRI has said the word certification.

policyExposure.regime: FERC large-load interconnection and co-location (ANOPR and technical conference)

policyExposure.regime: NERC large-load reliability standards and ride-through requirements
policyExposure.exposure: The 'Reliability Guideline: Risk Mitigation for Emerging Large Loads' (December 2025) and the August 2026 ride-through work ('improving consistency in ride-through requirements and developing testing and certification methodologies') are the technical inputs NERC and the system operators are drawing on; NERC President Jim Robb endorsed Flex MOSAIC ('having clear, technically grounded definitions of flexibility is critical for reliability'). If a NERC standard adopts EPRI's classes, EPRI's framework becomes de facto regulation it did not write as a regulator.

financials.commentary: EPRI is a member-funded 501(c)(3) that publishes audited consolidated statements each April and files a Form 990 each November; both were read for this dossier and both figures are stated where they differ by scope. The structure a reader can rely on: roughly 48 percent fixed membership dues from utilities, roughly 50 percent opt-in supplemental and contract funding (DCFlex, LCRI, federal awards), a small services and report-sales tail; nuclear is the largest sector at about 36 percent of expense; the institute ran deficits in 2023 and 2024 and a USD 6.65m surplus in 2025. Expectations are empty by design — no guidance, no consensus.

strategyRead: 1. **(High confidence)** We assess that EPRI's value to this corpus is as the convener that gets the gatekeepers and the gated into one room: DCFlex is the only standing forum in which the hyperscalers (Google, Meta, Microsoft, Oracle, NVIDIA), the landlords (Compass, QTS), the utilities (Duke, Dominion, Southern, Constellation, Vistra, NRG, PG&E) and the grid operators (ERCOT, PJM) co-fund demonstrations and co-author a framework. Basis: the founding roster of 29 October 2024, growth to 'more than 65' collaborators on Flex MOSAIC by March 2026, nine demonstration sites, and the fact that every one of those parties pays — the DCFlex notice prices a data-centre operator's seat at USD 325,000 a year.

2. **(High confidence)** We assess that EPRI is an advisor, not an assurance body, and that its new `assurance` seat is adjacent on a narrow basis: it writes the guidelines (ESIC's eighteen, the Reliability Guideline for Emerging Large Loads), runs the test methods (Energy Storage Test Manual, module burn tests) and keeps the incident database the certifiers and insurers cite — but it issues no certificate, listing or mark, holds no accreditation as a certification body, and has used the word 'certification' once, for ride-through 'testing and certification methodologies' it is still developing (August 2026). The seat rests on the testing-and-guidelines line only; if that ride-through work becomes an EPRI-run qualification, the basis strengthens.

3. **(High confidence)** We assess that the BESS failure statistics are EPRI's most consequential public product for the storage chain and that they should be quoted with their denominators: 97 percent decline 2018–2023 (9.2 to 0.2 incidents per GW), 98 percent to 2024, eight incidents worldwide in 2024, and '72% of failures in systems whose age is known occurred during construction, the commissioning process or within two years' — of 64 known-age incidents among 81 catalogued, with 26 root causes assigned. The kwh-analytics dossier's '72 percent within two years of installation' holds with that nuance; permitting dockets (CEC 25-OPT-02) now cite the figures directly.

4. **(Moderate confidence)** We assess that Flex MOSAIC is the deliverable most likely to change how this corpus's projects interconnect: a five-class flexibility taxonomy endorsed by NERC's and NARUC's presidents, with a final version due by October 2026 and PJM-era capacity rules the obvious adopter. The confidence is moderate because the framework is voluntary by design ('a technical foundation that jurisdictions and market participants can adapt'), and because the operators' appetite is contested on the record — Schneider's Carlini ('questionable whether they want to do it'), AES's Costa ('Data center operators do not like to be flexible') against EPRI's own measured 25 percent for three hours in Phoenix and 30–40 percent within seconds in London.

5. **(High confidence)** We assess that NVIDIA is structurally embedded in EPRI's AI agenda to a degree no other vendor is — DCFlex founder, OPAI model co-developer and NIM distributor, Flex MOSAIC collaborator, micro-data-centre partner, GPU supplier to every compute demonstration, and the board's one external technology director since April 2025. EPRI's 'we do not advocate for any specific company, sector, or technology' is the stated posture; the roster is the fact. A reader weighing OPAI's 'open' models should note that no open-weights release exists eighteen months after launch — the models remain NVIDIA NIM early access.

6. **(High confidence)** We assess that the identity facts the coverage plan carried were wrong in two places and the inbound count in one: EPRI is not a California corporation (DC domicile on every Form 990 through FY2024; a Delaware certificate now posted and a 2026 California foreign registration of the Delaware entity), Palo Alto is the principal office with Charlotte unverified as the largest site, and five dossiers, not three, cite EPRI. The FY2024 Form 990 (USD 503.2m revenue, 1,475 employees) and the FY2025 audited statements (USD 509.6m) are the figures to carry.

7. **(Moderate confidence)** We assess that governance turnover is the near-term risk to EPRI's convening role: the chair elected in May 2026 is leaving his utility in 2027 (Exelon 8-K, 25 August 2026); nine directors left the roster in 2025–26 including the CEOs of PG&E, Constellation, MISO and KHNP; and the Energy & Policy Institute's critique that 'the vast majority of its board members are utility executives' is accurate as a description. None of this touches the research, but DCFlex's neutrality claim depends on a board the hyperscalers trust, and that board is almost entirely their counterparties.

COLLECTION GAPS — (a) revenue by initiative: EPRI publishes no DCFlex, OPAI or FLEXIT budget and no member count by class; (b) the Delaware redomestication date — the certificate carries none in the extracted text and the FY2025 Form 990 (due November 2026) will be the first to show the new domicile; (c) whether the CMBlu pilot results were published; (d) litigation 2023–2026 — CourtListener was throttled and Justia blocked, so 'none found' is not 'none'; (e) which Flex MOSAIC class, if any, PJM or ERCOT adopts; (f) the 'largest office is Charlotte' claim — supported only by the Charlotte mailing address on the 2026 California registration; (g) no first-party photographs are published for any leader.

INDICATORS TO WATCH — the Flex MOSAIC final framework (due by October 2026) and the first ISO or state tariff that cites a MOSAIC class; the 96 MW Aurora site in Manassas going live 'late 2026' as the first flexibility-by-design build; the FY2025 Form 990 (November 2026) for the Delaware domicile, the FY2025 headcount and any change in the DOE award position; a chair transition at the 2027 board meeting following Innocenzo's Exelon departure; an Open Power AI open-weights release or a WattWorks benchmark of utility-trained models (tests whether 'open' means open); the next BESS Failure Incident Database annual update (2025 incident count and rate); and DCFlex's planned end 'by the end of 2027' — whether it is renewed, folded into a numbered programme, or spun into a standing body.
